Does anyone have any experience with this laser and any suggestions?

posts.author: Dinesh
posts.content_md:
> **Feng:** I have a holographic system with Coherent Sabre argon laser (3638 line) using two beams (one direct and one bounced from a mirror) interference to generate gratings of ~200nm pitch.Recently I start to see some intensity modulations on top of the grating (parallel to the grating) with much bigger pitch ~3/16".

There seems to be something a little odd with your numbers. I assume that the 3638 line means you're recording with 363.8nm, since you're using an argon laser. If the grating pitch is 200nm, then

sin(theta) = lambda/d = 363.8/200 > 1 ???

On the other hand, if the beams are counter-propagating, then:

d = lambda/(2n) => n = lambda/(2d) = 363.8/400 = 0.909 < 1 ???

If it is running in multimode, then the new gratings are coming in at the same angles as the original gratings and so:

lambda/d = m*lambda/d'

where d' is the new pitch. In this case the multimode multiplier, m, is (and we're expecting an integer): 

m = d'/d = (3/16)in/200nm = 4.76*(10)^(6)/200 = 23,800

So, multimode seems a little unlikely.

posts.author: BobH
posts.content_md:
I use a Sabre laser to make hologram gratings almost every day. The lines you're seeing don't indicate multimode operation. If the path lengths are not equalized, you'd just get no recording if that was the case. The coherence length of that laser is about 20mm without an etalon. By the way, TEMoo indicated does not mean the laser is running in single frequency mode. The only way to verify that is with a scanning Fabry-Perot interferometer, aka spectrum analyzer. 

I suspect that some of your light might be hitting the edge of the recording material, causing light to enter the edge and "waveguide" down it causing the lines of parasitic grating exposure. Mask off the edges and see if that fixes it.

posts.author: Dinesh
posts.content_md:
> **dcgman:** the proper equation to use for this set-up is d=lambda/(2*sin(theta))

It depends on whether it's a reflection geometry or a transmission geometry. If it's a reflection geometry then the formula is true only if the index of the recording material is unity. Inside a material, the wavelength shortens by the refractive index so that 

lambda_material = lambda_air/n

In this situation, the denominator needs to be modulated by the index since the spatial frequency is caused by the nodes in the standing wave pattern. You also need to be careful which theta you're using. The traditional approach is to measure the angle with respect to the plate normal. However, if the formula you quote is meant to be that pertaining to a reflection geometry (that is, counterpropagating beams), then if theta is measured with respect to the plate normal, then theta is zero and d becomes infinite; in this situation, theta needs to be measured from the plate parallel.

However the quoted formula can also be the formula for two beams in a transmission geometry (since, by Euler's formula, sin(-theta) = -sin(theta) ) where the beams are symmetrically arranged on either side of the plate normal. However:

> **Feng:** ...using two beams (one direct and one bounced from a mirror)

would seem to indicate a reflection geometry. If such is the case, then the former applies, so theta is to be measured to the plate parallel and the index needs to be taken into account.

So, if the geometry is a transmission with the two beams symmetrically arranged on either side of the plate normal, then the angle on either side of the plate normal would be 65 odd degrees. My impression of the description led me to believe that it was a reflection geometry with two counterpropagating beams, hence the statement of my assumption:

> **Dinesh:** On the other hand, if the beams are counter-propagating, then...

posts.author: dcgman
posts.content_md:
"Inside a material, the wavelength shortens by the refractive index so that 

lambda_material = lambda_air/n"

 YES!! -and inside the material the laws of refraction dictate that the sine of the angle of incidence gets divided by its refractive index. So the 'n's cancel in the equation describing Feng's set-up, giving the same 'd'. The geometry of the set-up in this particular case does not require one to take 'n' into consideration- the period of the fringe field set-up by the two interfering beams is the same in air and in the substrate.

posts.author: Dinesh
posts.content_md:
> **dcgman:** YES!! -and inside the material the laws of refraction dictate that the sine of the angle of incidence gets divided by its refractive index. So the 'n's cancel in the equation describing Feng's set-up, giving the same 'd'. The geometry of the set-up in this particular case does not require one to take 'n' into consideration- the period of the fringe field set-up by the two interfering beams is the same in air and in the substrate.

True, if the geometry were a transmission geometry. Then the n in the denominator due to the wavelength shortening would cancel the n due to the refraction

d = lambda/2*sin(theta) (1)

But, inside the material, the refracted beam makes an angle theta' given by,as you point out, sin(theta') = sin(theta)/n, and lambda'= lambda/n. So now:

d' = lambda'/2*sin(theta') = (lambda/n)/(2*sin(theta)/n) = n*(lambda/2*n*sin(theta)) =d 

And the n's do cancel out.

But, if the geometry were a reflection geometry with both beams hitting the plate head-on from opposite sides - a counterpropagating beam geometry - then there is no refraction, since the angle of incidence is normal. However, the wavelength is still shortened from lambda to lambda/n. The angles now need to be taken from the plate parallel (otherwise theta = 0) and

d = lambda/(n*2*sin(pi/2)) = lambda/(2*n) (2)

> **Feng:** using two beams (one direct and one bounced from a mirror)

But, where was the mirror?

If the mirror was directly "behind" the plate, ie the recording plate was between the light source and the mirror (assuming a collimated light source) and parallel to the mirror, or to put it perhaps more succinctly, the incoming k vector was directly opposed to the reflected beam, then there is no refraction because the beams are hitting the plate at normal incidence. Then the Bragg planes form along the nodes of the standing wave and these are at the (shortened) wavelength peaks. Well, actually the peaks of the square of the wavelength. In this case, equation 2 holds and the index needs to be taken into account..

If the light hit a beamsplitter and then a mirror with the beamsplitter and the mirror on the same side of the plate, that is, the beam hits the beamsplitter, then part of the beam passes through to the plate and part is reflected to a mirror which is tilted so as to direct the reflected beam onto the plate, you have a transmission geometry. In this geometry there is no need to take the index into account and equation 1 holds.

I assumed a reflection geometry from the description, in which case the numbers were odd. If the geometry were transmission, then your calculation is correct.

 The refractive index only plays a part in the calculation of the fringe density *if the beam actually refracts*. However, I made the assumption (*"..if the beams are counterpropagating."*), in which case the beam does not refract, since the angle of incidence is zero (Note for the sake of accuracy, that a Feynmann analysis using QED, would make it possible for a zero incidence beam to refract, since Fermat's Principle is classical - I just don't want someone searching the internet and finding somewhere that a zero angle of incidence beam does refract!).

So, based on the description:

 and the assumption (*"..if the beams are counterpropagating."*), there is no refraction, and hence the density of planes is given by the equation:

d = lambda/(2*n)

If Feng then went on to say that the geometry was indeed a transmission geometry, then clearly the assumption (remember, it was:*"..if the beams are counterpropagating."*) was also inaccurate. However, any calculation is based on the postulates by which that calculation is made; the calculation rests or falls on the basis of the postulates. This is the basis of the theory of measurement in the quantum regime. 

I hope that this makes it clear. There are several books in which the density of Bragg planes are given for two counterpropagating beams launched into a material. If the derivation of a mathematical calculation based on postulates and the succeeding epistemological value of such calculations interests you, I strongly suggest studying the Bohr-Einstein discussions.
